text: Sommer made his living as a lithographer and painted on his own time. He started as an apprentice in Detroit, where he was born, and later studied in Munich for a year. In 1907 he moved to Cleveland to work for Otis Lithograph, and there he helped found the Kokoon Arts Club, a bohemian group that met to paint, talk and drink. Offset printing took his job in 1929. After that he showed at the Whitney Biennial and the Museum of Modern Art. He liked farm scenes and young children.

Astrup failed his Latin exams because he was busy drawing, and that ended his father's plan to make him a priest. Born on the island of Frøya, he grew up in Jølster, where he lived and painted for most of his life. He studied in Oslo and Paris, then in Berlin under Lovis Corinth. His farm landscapes of western Norway use bold, strong colour, and people compare them with Munch's work. He also made woodcuts. Tuberculosis and asthma wore him down, and he died of pneumonia at 47.

Lockwood de Forest began as a landscape painter and became a designer of Indian-style interiors. As a young man he studied with Frederic Edwin Church, who was his mentor. His honeymoon in British India lasted two years. There he met a philanthropist in Ahmadabad, and together they opened a woodcarving workshop that supplied carved furniture and architectural woodwork to Tiffany's firm Associated Artists. He then ran his own decorating business for thirty years. After he retired he moved to Santa Barbara and went back to painting.

Francia's real name was Raibolini, and he made his living as a goldsmith and medallist in Bologna. He also directed the city mint. His earliest known painting, the Felicini Madonna, is dated 1494. He ran a large workshop, where Marcantonio Raimondi first learned to engrave. A story says Raphael's Santa Cecilia left him so depressed that he died of it. Historians now discard that tale, since the two men were friends.

Horthemels engraved copper plates in Paris for nearly fifty years and signed more than sixty of them. Her first published work, in 1707, was a frontispiece for Lesage's novel Le Diable boiteux. Engraving ran in the family. Her sister Marie-Anne-Hyacinthe married the engraver Nicolas-Henri Tardieu, and in 1713 she herself married the engraver Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Elder. Later plates carry her married name, Cochin. Their son became engraver to the court of Louis XV, and she died at his house in Paris.

Dietrich could imitate almost any old master, and that was both his talent and his trouble. At eighteen he finished a painting in two hours, and Augustus II of Saxony paid for him to study in Italy and the Netherlands. Winckelmann called him the Raphael of landscape. Some of his Rembrandt-style pictures in Dresden carry fake dates and Rembrandt's name. In 1741 he became court painter there, on condition that he deliver four cabinet pictures a year. He never developed a style of his own.

Raphael became Perugino's most famous pupil. Perugino himself came from Città della Pieve, and his nickname only says that he worked in Perugia. Scholars still argue about whether his family was poor or rich, and nobody knows his exact birth date. Vasari says he trained in Verrocchio's workshop next to Leonardo. About 1480 Pope Sixtus IV called him to Rome to paint frescoes on the Sistine Chapel walls. He was also one of the first central Italian painters to work in oil.

Medicine came first for Carus, and painting second. In 1814 he became professor of obstetrics in Dresden, and in the same years he taught himself oil painting while working under Caspar David Friedrich. He also wrote on art theory. His own idea of landscape painting was to show the inner workings of the earth, and he called it Erdlebenbildkunst. Goethe was his friend. In 1844 he travelled through Britain as personal physician to the King of Saxony, and Queen Victoria hosted them at Windsor Castle.

Lemoyne taught both Natoire and François Boucher. He won the Prix de Rome in 1711 and went to Italy to study, and later he became a professor at the Académie and first painter to Louis XV. His rival for the title of leading painter of his generation was Jean-François de Troy. Contemporaries called Lemoyne the new Le Brun, and he did much of his best work at Versailles. He killed himself in 1737, at the height of his career.

Neumann grew up very poor, but Veit Hanns Schnorr von Carolsfeld liked his work and took him on as a student at the Academy of Fine Arts. His father worked as a colorist and his brother became a wood engraver. Neumann later worked in the studio of the copper engraver Henry Winkles. Many of his portraits were printed in Die Gartenlaube and the Illustrirte Zeitung. He was best known for portraits of musicians, including Franz Schubert and Robert Franz.

Elias Martin's carpenter father wanted his son in the trade, but the boy preferred art and became an apprentice to a Swedish court painter. A job designing ship ornaments led him to Augustin Ehrensvärd, who took him to the sea fortress of Sveaborg for two years. In 1766 Martin went to Paris and tried to copy Boucher, but the style did not suit him. He moved on to London. Nationalencyklopedin calls him Sweden's first great landscape painter.

Vereshchagin graduated first in his class at the naval school and then left the service right away to study drawing. In Paris he studied under Gérôme, though he disagreed with his methods. In 1867 he joined a Russian army expedition to Central Asia. His courage at the siege of Samarkand won him the Cross of St. George. As a war artist he painted realist scenes so graphic that many were never printed or shown to the public.

Hardly anything is known about Correggio's early life. His real name was Antonio Allegri, and his birth date is a guess of about 1489. He was probably apprenticed in Modena, where he would have met the work of Francesco Francia. Dynamic compositions and steep foreshortening made him an early sign of the Baroque. He is considered a master of chiaroscuro. Correggio led the Parma school of the High Renaissance.

Nothing is known for certain about Van der Goes before 1467, when he became a master in the painters' guild of Ghent. Some historians guess that Dieric Bouts was his teacher, but there is no evidence. He painted the Adoration of the Magi, now in Berlin, and worked on an altarpiece ordered by the banker Tommaso Portinari. That Portinari Altarpiece reached Florence in 1483, after the painter had already died. It helped shape realism and the use of colour in Italian Renaissance art.

Davies trained as a lawyer and ended up making the Norfolk Broads famous. He was the eldest child of a geologist. In 1871, just after qualifying, he read an account of the Broads and applied to join a law practice in Norwich. He became a prolific photographer and writer there. His books include The Swan and Her Crew, which follows three young naturalists and sportsmen through the Broads and rivers of Norfolk.

Born in Belgium, Haes became one of the three grand masters of Spanish landscape painting. In 1857 he was named the first professor of landscape painting at the Royal Academy of San Fernando in Madrid. He was the first in Spain to teach painting straight from nature. His pupil Aureliano de Beruete became a landscape master too. In 1876 the Spanish state bought his view of the Canal of Mancorbo in the Picos de Europa for the Prado.

A goldsmith's son and one of nine children, Parreiras left the Imperial Academy in Rio after two years to study with the German immigrant Georg Grimm. In 1886 Emperor Pedro II bought one of his works. That let him go back to formal study and sail to Europe, where he trained in Venice under Filippo Carcano. Home again, he taught landscape painting and followed Grimm by taking his students outdoors to paint. After disagreements over the curriculum, he opened a school of his own, the Escola do Ar Livre.

Lam Qua painted Western-style portraits mostly for Western clients, and he was the first Chinese portrait painter shown in the West. His workshop stood in New China Street among the Thirteen Factories in Canton. Some contemporaries said he studied with George Chinnery, though Chinnery denied it. Lam Qua charged less than Chinnery. From 1836 to 1855 he painted patients of Peter Parker, an American medical missionary who ordered pictures of people with large tumors before their operations. Some of those paintings are now at Yale.

Monkeys made Mori Sosen famous. Robert van Gulik called him an undisputed master of painting the Japanese macaque. He also painted deer, boars and peafowl. When the Dutch brought a gibbon to Japan in 1809, nobody there had seen a live one for centuries, and Mori made a picture record of the event. Nobody knows whether he was born in Osaka, Nagasaki or Nishinomiya, but he lived in Osaka most of his life.

Sesson came from the Satake clan, but his father disinherited him and he became a Zen monk at Shōsō-ji temple. He took the character for snow in his name from Sesshū, whom he admired, though some scholars doubt that Sesshū shaped his painting. In Ibaraki he is called "Sesshū of the west, Sesson of the east". He painted landscapes such as Eight Views of Xiaoxiang and legendary figures like Li Tieguai. Twice he went to Aizu to teach painting to the daimyō Ashina Moriuji.
